utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before I invite the Prosecution to call its next witness, I'm addressing you, Mr. Waespi, in relation to the previous witness, the Chamber noticed that two documents which were announced as being attached to the witness statement have not been dealt with during his testimony and the Chamber wonders whether you are still seeking to have these admitted, that is 65 ter 3187, and 65 ter 2372 as listed under numbers 13 and 14 in your 28th of May, 2008 submission of Rule 92 ter statements and associated exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sure that they are not needed. The reason probably but I'll check over the break, is that they were already admitted by another witness or we decided it's not relevant. I think one of them was outside the indictment period, but I will check and give you a definite answer after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you on that matter. Apart from that, if there are no other procedural issues, I would like to invite the Prosecution and will it be you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Yes, it will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will take the next witness. Your next witness would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Witness 106, Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And Your Honours, in the meantime, if I may say that there are a few administrative matters that we would like to deal with but we can do it at the end of the testimony of the witness as regarding previous witnesses and their specific requests made by the Chamber with respect to these previous witnesses. It shouldn't take more than five minutes but just so that the Chamber is aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then you also asked us to give permission to add three witness-related documents to the Rule 65 ter exhibit list. I do understand that there is no objection against that from the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With regard to Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then permission is given so the request is granted to add these to the 65 ter list. Good morning, Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to give a solemn declaration that you will spec the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. Mr. Usher now hands out to you the text of the solemn declaration and I'd like you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly swear that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, please be seated, Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dijkstra, the Chamber was informed that you had some problem with your shoulder which is confirmed by your appearance at this moment. We were asked to have breaks a bit earlier than usual, that is, after approximately one hour. If there is any moment where you feel uncomfortable as far as your physical condition is concerned, and please do not hesitate to address me, and we'll seek to accommodate your needs.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Dijkstra. Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Switbertus Johannes Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what is your current occupation?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I'm a Major in the Netherlands air force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could I please ask Mr. Usher to provide hard copies of the statement to the witness. Major Dijkstra, do you recall providing a witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor on the 7 December, 1995?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Could we please have 65 ter 4923 on the screen and did you have a chance to review this statement before today?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And it's going to come up on the screen in a few seconds. And when it does, can you please confirm that the statement you see on the screen is the one that we just have discussed?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That is the same one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 4924, please. And Mr. Dijkstra, do you remember providing a supplemental witness statement to the Office of the Prosecutor that you signed on the 12th March, 2008 based on an interview on the 6th of December, 2007?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And do you remember looking at that statement before today?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Is that the statement that we see on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That is the same one, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do these two statements accurately reflect to the Office of the Prosecutor in the course of those interviews?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Are the contents of those statements that you signed true to the best of your knowledge and recollection?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And if you were asked the same questions in court today that you were asked in the course of those interviews, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, I would like to have 65 ter 4923 and 4924 admitted into evidence under Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From the written submissions, I do understand that there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There are no objections to the admission. It's my only comment on them Judge is consistent with the Chamber's comments about the witness' opinions that they are -- they are not part of the factual aspects here. We didn't go through and redact those portions because of those efforts so while I don't object to the admission, of course giving Your Honour's prior guidance on opinions, they are -- the admission is to facts and what he saw and facts that he observed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if any conclusions are drawn from the observations of a witness, it's not necessarily that the Chamber draws the same conclusions as the witness did. At the same time, you could exclude that the Chamber would draw the same conclusions but then always on the totality of the evidence and not just on the basis and because the witness drew such conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This being on the record, Mr. Registrar, the 1995 statement of Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 04923 and it becomes Exhibit P428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P428 is admitted into evidence. The next statement is the 2007 -- December 2007 and 12th of March 2008 statement would be ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is 65 ter 04924 and becomes P429.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P429 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Dijkstra, when I address you as Mr. Dijkstra rather as Major Dijkstra, that is not in any way out of disrespect for the rank you are holding but because that's how I usually address witnesses, that is, without specific reference to a rank or position. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, I would also like to have admitted into evidence 65 ter 4925, 4926, and 4927 which are exhibits to the supplemental statement of Major Dijkstra and since the foundation is laid in there, I would like to have those admitted as well, pursuant to the 92 ter submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand from the written submissions that there are no objections, it's mainly marking and further clarification. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 04925 becomes Exhibit P430. 65 ter number 04926 becomes Exhibit P431. And 65 ter number 04927 becomes P432.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P430, P431 and P43 are admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, there is an additional document that is referred to in the witness statement but that is not an exhibit to the statement. It is not of critical importance to the Prosecution but since the statement is now admitted, we can also admit that document which is a report made by Major Dijkstra on the 8th of August, it's at paragraph 30 of his is supplemental statement, and I don't know -- if that's something that the Chamber would like to have as well. We have it as 65 ter number 5199.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You intend to tender this from the bar table as it's often called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It's just a situation where it was not an exhibit so to have the evidence in the statement admitted with the specific reference to a document which is not on the record may be -- may not be a helpful to the Trial Chamber so that's the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think we can clear to this up at the break if I can look at this document, I can probably just give a quick glance to it and get past it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then the Chamber will further hear from the parties in this respect. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: At this time, I would like to read out a short summary of the evidence of the witness contained in the two witness statements and the witness has been informed of the purpose of this exercise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Major Dijkstra was a United Nations Military Observer in Sector South in 1995. He was stationed in Benkovac until 26 July 1995 after which date, he became a logistics officer stationed in Knin at the UNMO headquarters where he stayed until 1 December 1995. He observed how there was a lack of heavy weapons, trenches or defence positions in Knin prior to Operation Storm. Major Dijkstra heard the shelling of Knin start at 5.00 a.m. on 4 August 1995. He was sleeping at the time and was awoken by the sound of rockets coming from multiple rocket launchers also called MRLs. After being taken to the UN compound at around 7.00 a.m., he continued to observe the shelling from the third-floor balcony. Major Dijkstra heard the shelling again on the 5th of August starting at 5.20 a.m. and heard one shell in the course of the morning impacting close to the UN camp. He saw that it had destroyed a cart and that about six people had been killed by that shell. When Major Dijkstra was allowed to come out of the UN camp on the 8th of August, he noticed that the town had been completely ransacked. He was surprised to see a large discrepancy between the heavy shelling he had heard and the relatively little damage he saw. In the course of the following weeks, he observed looting and arson including looting and arson committed by soldiers in military vehicles. This concludes my summary, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Major Dijkstra, I just want to ask you a few questions to clarify what was said in your two statements that I just summarised. My first questions relate to your time in Benkovac. So up to 26 July, 1995. If we can have 65 ter number 5186, please, on the screen. Now, in your statement, Major Dijkstra, you stated that there were some military barracks just outside of town on the road to Rastevic. Do you remember making that statement and remember those barracks?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: If I can have the assistance of Mr. Usher to help Mr. Dijkstra locate, if he can, where the location of those barracks are.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Forgive me, I'm truly right-handed but this should be, as far as I remember, somewhere in this region and coming from Benkovac on the right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Dijkstra. Would you be able to write letters MB for military barracks or am I asking you too much?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, you were, if the usher can just write it for him where he wants it that would be just as easy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We leave it to Mr. Dijkstra, whether he feels comfortable to do it or not. If you need assistance, you'll let us know, Mr. Dijkstra.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You better do it, it's not going to work. So just in the circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And MB stands for?

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Military barracks. If we could have that admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P433, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P433 is admitted into evidence. The no objections from Mr. Kehoe did not appear on the transcript but repeated by me, they now do. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we can have Exhibit D248 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Major Dijkstra, what you will see on the screen in a few seconds is a map of Benkovac prepared by the Defence on which they have listed a number of locations on it. As soon as we have it, I'll ask you about some of those locations and if we can go to page 3 of that document when it's up, Mr. Registrar, please. Thank you. First of all, let me ask you on this picture you see in front of you, how is the military barracks that you have just identified on the previous map, how is it described here?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: It's described as B Macura barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And looking at this map it's at the approximately same location as you marked on the other map, and it's consistent with your recollection?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Looking at that location, that should be the same barracks that I described in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Looking at these other locations on the map, for example let's start at the bottom where it says communication centres of the 3rd brigade of the ARSK and right underneath, command of the 3rd brigade ARSK do you remember that these facilities existed at that time in Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: What about what is labelled as the fireman's hall defence office, do you remember that facility being in the location where it's described on this map?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I can't be positive. I've been to Benkovac after 1995 and I see the fireman's hall there and that looked new so I can't be positive that that would be the same one if it's in the same location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just with some clarity, Your Honour, if we look at the question, the question is does he know or does he remember? I mean the question is does he know. I think that's what Your Honours and the Chamber want to know. Does he know about these facilities or not know about these facilities and the question was a bit -- does he remember and I think the issue here is one of knowledge. Does he know that those facilities were there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hedaraly, the issue is whether the witness would know at this moment, then of course there must be some moment of remembrance anyhow because he's not at Benkovac at this moment but you are invited to ask the witness not only whether he remembers from those times when he was there but if he knows anything about the existence of those locations at a later stage. Nevertheless, it is good for us to know whether his knowledge stems from the time he was there or whether his knowledge stems from any other source and whether he gained his knowledge at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Major Dijkstra, do you remember -- I'm sorry, do you know whether there was a building a facility called the JNA centre at the location where it's identified on the map?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I ask you the same question about the post office, the police station, the hotel, and you can take each of them in turn?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I know there was a police station, but looking at the situation from the police station regarding to the hotel, I can't be positive if we are talking about the same police station that I remember. I can't remember being a post office because we never used the post office for sending mail. The JNA centre I can't remember. The nun's convent not. And what is it, the FCP of the 7th corps, I can't remember -- oh sorry, that's in the barracks location; so the only thing I actually can remember and have heard of at that time was the fireman's hall and that should be around that location and the barracks then, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, how was that fireman's hall being used, if you know and/or if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I only heard it being referred to as the fireman's hall, maybe somebody referred it as -- I say it -- a centre for emergency dispatching -- how you call it, a call centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you do not know exactly how to call it in English, I might be able to assist you because I speak the same language as you do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Dutch spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, now this is not caught by the -- I think the witness said that in Dutch, "You would call it the centre room where all the messages come in and from where control is exercised over what has to be done." I know that this is not the real procedure as he we usually have it in court. If there's at any moment any doubt, just try to give the Dutch name rather than -- because whatever you add to that, our transcribers and our interpreters will be lost.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you for the translation, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now when you say it was the call centre where the message would be received, are you talking when there are fires, emergency calls being made or are we talking about --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the leading. I object to the leading. Just -- the witness said what it was. I object to the leading from counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't really understand what he meant by the call centre where messages were received. I'm just trying to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the building was called the fireman's hall, Mr. Hedaraly, may I is ask the witness whether it was specifically for the purposes of reporting fires or whether it had any broader use. Please proceed, Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you answer the question or do you want me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I -- well, it will be an assumption, because nobody clearly told me they said it's a fireman's hall and a call centre so from my own experience in the military, and in the Dutch system, that should be the call centre where the calls for fire or emergency come in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It comes down, if you say, "I'm assuming this" then it comes down to speculation. Let's refrain from that. Mr. Hedaraly, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Were there any, staying in the city of Benkovac -- we don't need the map anymore -- were there any ARSK soldiers in the town of Benkovac itself?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, there were soldiers in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were these soldiers in organised units or were they individual soldiers?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: As far as I have seen them, they were individual soldiers. I haven't seen any group formations during my time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what was these individual soldiers that you would see in town, what would you observe them doing?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Well, if I may put it simply, doing their daily business, shopping, walking around, sitting at bars or cafes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And were these individual ARSK soldiers that you saw in Benkovac, to your knowledge, did they live in the town of Benkovac?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That's a difficult question because I haven't spoken to any of them individually, at least not from the ones I saw in town. But it looked like --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to any answer. It's pure speculation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, he can answer based on his observations even if he hasn't spoken to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is not asking for speculation as such. The witness could have knowledge of it although he started telling us that he didn't speak with any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He might have checked the population registers --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand it's possible. I didn't consider that possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. No it's not the most likely possibility but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I mean the point is that he can have knowledge other than by speaking to them. His observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel, counsel, please. I mean if we go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You triggered this more or less, Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- by objecting. Please proceed. Let's just hear the answer of the witness. The question was, Mr. Dijkstra -- I even have to scroll back for the question. The question was whether these individual ARSK soldiers that you saw, whether they were, to your knowledge, whether they lived in the town of Benkovac. And you started your answer by saying it's a difficult question. It appeared to be. Please, tell us your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like I said, I haven't spoken to them, but the way they behaved when I observed them, they either lived in town or close by. They did their shopping there. They were sitting in bars, talking to -- not only to other guys in military uniform but also to civilians. I seen them walking around with women and with kids so that's how I assumed that at least a great deal of them lived in the town or in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I want to refer now to your time in Knin and in paragraph 10 of your supplemental witness statement, you mention that ARSK soldiers in Knin were rotating that they were on leave. Do you recall that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can you please tell the Court whether these ARSK soldiers that you saw in Knin were individual soldiers or soldiers as -- there as part of an organised units?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Most of the soldiers I saw, let me say almost all the soldiers I saw were acting as individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have P430 on the screen, please, and that was the attachment to the witness statement that was just admitted a few moments ago. Major Dijkstra, I'm going to show you the aerial photo of Knin that you have identified when you -- that you have marked when you made your witness statement and I just have one very specific question on it just to clarify something. In your statement, you identified locations labelled on the map as 3 and 4 as the government building and radio station?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And you circle a portion of the town. I just want to clarify: Is this the whole -- I mean is this entire area the government building and the radio station or are those two buildings within that area?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Those two buildings should be within that area, but it's difficult for this aerial photograph to identify them. I never saw them from above, I always saw them from, say, the town side. So looking up the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to refer to paragraph 17 of your witness statement where you state that you clearly recalled hearing multiple racket launchers at 5 a.m. on the 4th of August and that those woke you up. My question is and could you tell the Chamber, how could you distinguish between the sounds of rockets from a multiple rocket launcher as opposed to a sound from a regular shell?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: The thing I heard that woke me up made a sound as I will describe it to people mostly like a train blowing its whistle inside a tunnel so it's almost a deafening sound. I admit I'm not an artillery guy so it is not my best field of experience but I've been on fire -- at fire ranges before and heart bullets, grenades, passing and they make a totally different sound, they make a sound like a whiz so my first assumption was this was something bigger. Knowing a bit about the arsenal that warring parties have, my first assumption was that it was a rocket from an MRLS and this was later confirmed by my roommate who had spent before he came to Knin half a year in Sarajevo and had met with those systems before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Major Dijkstra. In -- I will now move to paragraph 33 of your supplemental witness statement and you talk about the very little structural damage to the town of Knin. Now, the damage that you did in fact observe, was it concentrated around the military targets that you identified in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, they were not -- they were, as far as I could see from what I have observed, all over town and not just concentrated around those targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Now, you -- I mean you heard at the beginning of -- before -- when your statement was being admitted, some objections and discussion about the opinions in your statement. You expressed an opinion that the way the military operation was conducted and particularly the shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Can I please finish, I'm going to ask him about the basis of his opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, let's first, before you answer the question, please make a pause. Mr. Hedaraly, you may finish your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like, if I could finish my question before an objection is made, I think that's usually the protocol how it works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, unless of course the question starts in such a way that I would say the harm is done before an objection can be made. Please keep this in mind and please ask your -- this or the same question not necessarily in the same words again. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: As you have heard from the Presiding Judge, the opinions that you provide in your statement are not necessarily of assistance to the Court so I want to ask you about the underlying facts that you observed or that you heard that help you form these opinions. So my question is: What are the underlying facts that you observed or heard that helped you form the opinion that the way in which the military operation was conducted and particularly the shelling was to get the people out? Before you answer, there may be an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, even the structure of that, I mean if we're just asking what did you see and what did you hear? I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then he say I saw the sun rising in the morning and of course you have to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I understand you have to direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly focuses the witness on what he expressed in some respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as an opinion and to ask him what are the facts that are at the basis of this opinion which might not necessarily assist the Chamber and that is a fair question. I mean he doesn't lead the witness into a conclusion because the conclusion is already there on paper, so what we are trying to find out is what are the facts underlying this opinion. Mr. Dijkstra, when you answer this question, could you really limit yourself to facts as you did before by saying I saw soldiers with women and children, not necessarily that these were their own wives and their own children but at least that's a fact that you observed which led you to conclusions and it could have been other conclusions as well but please try to focus on the facts on which you based these opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Do you want me to repeat the question or is it clear to you?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: One of the first facts was that the amount of shelling I heard, the heaviness I heard when I was woken up and spent the first two hours in my house then went through town to the barracks and from the barracks, observed an heard the shelling going on for the remainder of 4th of August and again on the 5th gave me a feeling that there was quite a lot falling on the town. So from that aspect, I was expecting to find a lot of damaged houses, destroyed houses. After the 8th of August, I stayed in Knin for the rest of my time and my living was close to what I marked on the map as the logistics base, and the damage I observed during that time was not consistent as far of what I would have expected to find. I hardly saw any completely destroyed house or heavily damaged house. I found some potholes that looked like from grenades. At one point I came to an apartment building that had a hole all the way on top or on its roof that looked like from some sort of projectile, but I didn't see any of what I expected observing the heaviness of the shelling. Another fact, although it's a hearsay fact, I have to admit, that after the war and after my time with the UN, I still had contact with some people from the Krajina and they told me that there has been an evacuation order almost straight after beginning of the shelling and also they were surprised that they could flee the country without much resistant and opposition. So those two facts, to me, probably drew my conclusion was this whole shelling was aimed to get the people out as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: In paragraph 36 of your supplemental statement, you describe looting that was done by people in military uniforms carrying non-military goods in military vehicles. My question for you is: How were you able to know that these were military vehicles?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: The vehicles of the Croatian army have -- you can say a military licence plate normally starting with two numbers then the letters HV, hotel Victor and three numbers. And all these cars I described as military vehicles for having those licence plates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And finally, Major Dijkstra, in paragraph 40 of your supplemental witness statement, you discuss an incident that you personally observed. You say that you saw an anti-aircraft gun mounted on a truck that was firing horizontally at houses. Can you please describe for the Court where this was and what you specifically observed?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Okay. I was on the road from Knin to Drnis with two colleague UNMOs and we observed on the right side of that road, so that's to the west, a military vehicle with a yellow licence plate. It was too far away to see if it was an HV registration but the civilian licence plates in Croatia are black of letters on white and the military are black letters on yellow, wearing a Puma insignia on its side firing a double-barrel anti-aircraft gun on houses that were even further to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And what kind of buildings, houses or structures were they firing at?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, these were civilian houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: And could you observe the people that were on the truck? Could you identify them?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I could only identify them as wearing -- military personnel because they wore military clothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hedaraly. Mr. Kehoe, may I take it that you will be the first to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I receive any indication as far as timing is concerned and I'm also addressing other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Sorry Judge I don't think it should be too long. If this could be an appropriate time for the Major to take a break before we go into that or do you ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we do not take a break now, Mr. Dijkstra, we most likely would go on for let's say half an hour. If you would say that's too much, then we'll have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm perfect. No problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Kehoe, then again my question which you skillfully evaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Judge, you brought me back to -- an hour or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I hear from other Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour, I suspect unless anything arises in Mr. Kehoe's cross-examination, we won't have any questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the -- Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I could estimate my cross-examination within an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Dijkstra, you see that the chances of being released from this place this morning are growing. Mr. Kehoe, please proceed. Mr. Kehoe is counsel for Mr. Gotovina and he will now cross-examine you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Good morning, Major.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Major, I would just like to go back and like to cover several questions that were addressed by the Prosecution and several matters that came up during the course of your witness statements, so if I bounce around a little bit, that's where I'm going. If you can just take a look again at D248. Major, just a clarifying question that you brought up on direct examination concerning the two items at the bottom of the page, the communications centre as well as the command of the 3rd Infantry Brigade of the ARSK. Is it your testimony that you didn't know those particular items were there?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, going back -- we're going to turn our attention away from Benkovac and back to Knin, and without going through it chapter and verse, I know that you just came to Knin shortly before Operation Storm. Just talking about some of the items in your statement and if I can direct your attention to your 2008 statement 429 in paragraph 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, perhaps before you continue, could you help us out? Of course the scale is indicated but not just in numbers which as soon as you enlarge it or reduce it in size then of course it's not valid anymore and we have to -- could I take it that the squares we find on this map which is the approximately three and a half to four in the width of this map and approximately two and a half from top to bottom, are these square kilometres?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This was a map that came up during the direct-examination or cross-examination of a protected witness with Mr. Misetic, if we can just check at the break and we'll get back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if you look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that we had a technical problem which now has been resolved. Yes. Mr. Kehoe, therefore, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I thought it would be square kilometres comparing more or less the proportions of the different things we find there such as streets, et cetera. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're just going back to your 2008 statement which is P429, and I would like to direct your attention to 15, paragraph 15 and you noted that with respect to the train line, I said in my previous statement that it was not a legitimate military target because it was not in use. Did you know, sir, whether those tracks were in fact usable?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention to -- the Court has heard testimony about an armoured train that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, if you wouldn't mind. What we are in at this moment is that this witness has given what clearly is judgement or an opinion about whether the rail track is a military target, yes or no. That is for the Chamber to decide finally and not for a witness. He also explained until now that's the sole basis for his judgement that he never, I think, until the end of October, he saw any of these rail tracks used. I mean that's the -- from what I understand, the sole basis for this judgement. Whether he would change his opinion, if he would know about armoured trains or tourist trains or anything else is not -- of course the Chamber knows because it has heard evidence on that train, I think even about the rail track being used by Mr. Tudjman briefly after Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: There is also the evidence of the ARSK using it to move items.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. There is a lot of evidence but why educate the witness or give him all kinds of information then ask him whether he would have a different judgement which is still for the Chamber to be made and not for the witness if he would have had other information which apparently he did not have or perhaps he has had it, but he has not considered it when drawing these conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then the item, Your Honour, with the consideration is for instance on Stara Straza, where did he observe railway cars going to the munitions depot at Stara Straza.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can ask him whether he knows any factual things and whether he has considered this but let's not try to give him all kind of information and then see whether that would cause him to make a different judgement on the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just before the Benkovac map is off the screen, we've been advised that it is 1 kilometre by 1 kilometre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Major, during the course of the time prior to Operation Storm, did you observe the RSK moving munitions to the ammunitions depot in Stara Straza?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: To be honest, I don't even know what Stara Straza is, or where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- is so you couldn't tell us about any movements of logistics at all?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you noted for us just a few things about the shelling and I just wanted to ask a follow-up on a couple of questions about the shelling. In paragraph 21 of your statement, and if we could go to P431. Now, the locations that you were -- if we can just blow up where those circles are. Now, those are the locations on the balconies that you were looking into Knin on both the 4th and the 5th; is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And you noted that while you were on these balconies, you couldn't see what was either targeted or hit; is that not correct? And I'm pointing you to the -- your statement on the paragraph 21 of P429.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And likewise, you were in no position to know whether there was outgoing RSK fire?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Also true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, obviously you talked just generally about the noise that was involved and the direction. And if we could go back to P430. Then if we could blow up the area that is in the right hand portion, Mr. Usher, the area that's pointed number 6. The area that you have circled as number 6, Major, is the area where you believe that the weaponry landed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Some of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let me turn your attention to a -- looking at the angles the way you were, let me turn your attention to -- if I may, I just get the number correct. 1D31-0003. While this is coming up, Major, this is just a different aerial with a bit of a different angle of fire.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Observation, excuse me. Now, Major, the bottom part of the chart with the X is the UN base. Is that the approximate location of the balconies where you were making your observations?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: They should be on the right hand corner of that eclipse.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The right-hand corner of the eclipse. And were these numbers of the general direction of where you saw the this fire going into or to the extent you could see it?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Sorry, I can't answer that positively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to -- Mr. Kehoe, were these numbers, I see some numbers in some --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: These numbers are the same numbers we had on the prior exhibit with Colonel Leslie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, no, but I'm just trying to understand were these numbers of the general direction of where you saw this fire going --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Toward.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then the witness said I can't answer that positively. Could you explain why you can't answer that but could you answer it negatively or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Also not us, because I have seen shells hit in those areas but these things are going is so fast it's difficult to tell from where they are coming and where they are going. You only see them land. So then it's difficult to say are all the shells going to the same direction. You just see some of them land in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, was that exactly because the area you marked on the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The area I marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The previous map is from what I see is by far, as far as distance is concerned, closer to the UN compound, it more or less covers the area in between the UN compound and the markings we see at this moment on this map in black. Now, when we are talking about shells landing, I take it, Mr. Kehoe, but just correct me when I am wrong, that one of the questions that was on your mind is whether where the witness indicated the area where the shells had landed, whether he could have been mistaken by looking in the same direction that the shells actually would have landed further away from the UN compound so not in the area you marked on that map, but rather on the areas as marked on this map. I take it that that's the issue you wanted to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, that's the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it took me to while to understand from your question that this was the issue. Have you now understood what the issue is, and could you tell us when you marked the area where you say the shells fell, which is an area which apparently at least has the look of an agricultural area rather than a built-up area. Is there any way that you may have -- that you are mistaken in the sense that the shells although you saw them landing in the same direction from where you were that it was rather in the town in the areas, the black areas numbered on this map rather than in the area you marked on the map earlier? That's the question, whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, the transcript says fells -- I believe you said fells and I think you meant shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Shells, I take it yes. I think I said that the shells fell but -- I think I said the shells but -- my question, although rather long, could you please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it is not really agricultural, it's more a swampy kind of area just next to the Krka River. Apart from that, I could hear the shells that close, I could also incidentally see them actually -- well sort of explode in that swampy land, so that's what gave me the conclusion since that is absolutely no target area, it is getting quite a bit of hits. And so it's difficult to say if they were short falls or whether it was deliberately target on there, short falls meaning shells not reaching where they actually had to go -- oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, could you give us any impression as to the number of I mean was that one or five or two where you had sound reasons for yourself to believe that they fell in this swampy area rather than further away on any of the -- in any of the areas indicated on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, looking at me as a person, I would say at least one every 15, 20 minutes to make such a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You mean landing --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Landing in that field and then saying from they get quite a few hits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just offered this item into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D392, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D392 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just, Major, turning your attention to an item you mentioned just what you heard and the noise I think on direct testimony you talked about the noise from what you believed to be MRLs. Let me show you a perspective, I'd like to show you two aerial perspectives, if I may, 1D31-0001. Now, this is an aerial photograph, Major, of looking into the UN camp. We've noted the TVIK factory, the railway, and the railway maintenance just to give some perspective. If you look at this, Major, the camp was backed up into -- and had several hilly or mountainous areas behind it, did you not just see that from the photo -- from the sketch. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: This comes from south to south-west and ... this is looking from the other direction with those -- a few different items. We have the UN camp down, TVIK factory, the railway, the hospital, and the railway maintenance. Now, Major, when the shelling came in, and to the extent that you would hear it in the UN camp, the fact that these mountains, it was down in this area at the base of these mountains or hills, that would cause an echo effect and the noise to be louder, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I'm not an expert, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: The question started a long time ago about when he believed he heard MRLs and I believe the witness's testimony that when he is sure he heard it was 5.00 a.m. in the morning of the 4th when he was not in the UN camp but when he was at home, so I think there is a confusion built in that question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's one issue. And of course the witness started to already answer the question that he's not an expert in these matters. It is a thought that came on to my mind as well whether you need expert knowledge but if there is anything that would be knowledge of every person and also keeping in mind what Mr. Hedaraly said, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, the knowledge of every person concerning ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I mean, the common knowledge of everyone would be that if you start, I think, singing in the mountains that there is some echo, that's clear. The same would be clear if you have ever heard people during hunting in the mountains, but then of course the next question to come is what would have been the impact on observations and that is a far more complex matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please keep that in mind and also keep in mind that Mr. Hedaraly said that you were confusing the position from where he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And I was attempting to focus the witness just at the time you were in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I take it, Major, your answer would be the same about the impact of this when you were in the UN camp?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's first try to then establish: When you were in the camp, did you hear similar sounds as you described earlier? I think you were talking about a train in a tunnel and that this was confirmed by your roommate. Now, did you hear is similar sounds when you were in the compound?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, especially on the morning of the 5th at the start again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time we'll offer 1D13-0001 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: Based on what has transpired, I don't see what the foundation is for this. If it's just to show that the area is hilly I don't think the Prosecution has any objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes, Mr. Hedaraly, objections on what is obvious take more time than just admitted into evidence because it doesn't harm in any way the Prosecution's case that it is a hilly area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: It doesn't, Your Honour, but I just don't want the record to be cluttered with documents that have -- that doesn't assist the Chamber, but I will withdraw the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we should take care that this will not happen. At the same time, we hear that you have no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D393, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D393 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Major, I just move to the rate of shelling that you were talking about and if I could just take a look at P101. Just the top of that page, Mr. Registrar. This is an UNMO report, Major, and it is on the 4th of August, at 12.05 and it notes the rate of shelling as of 10.40. And it notes that the HV shelling on Knin started at the 4th of August at 0500 and continued to 10.20 and up to 10.20, the rate of fire was 350 to 400 artillery MRL rocket fire were heard. Is that approximately your recollection, those numbers?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I have to say I haven't counted them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay, sir. Let me move to paragraph 28 of your 2008 statement. And if you can, sir, and this has to do with the -- your observations of the Croatian soldiers coming in on the 5th and you noted: "As I stated, I could see the Croatian troops coming into town from the south at about noon on 5.00 [sic] on the same road from Drnis ..." is excuse me -- "around noon on the 5th, that's the 5th of August on the same road from Drnis. I couldn't see other directions from the balcony so I don't know if other troops entered the town from other roads." Now, based on that, sir, you had come to a conclusion that these soldiers were coming into an unarmed town; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That's not what I concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You didn't conclude that?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Not on those basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Did you know that -- let's go to D334. Now, if this is a statement of the ECMM of 12.45. And it notes in the third item that at 11.15 hours -- these items were met at the entrance and this is the entrance to the hospital by the HV. Do you see that at 11.15? It's in number 3. Maybe we could just blow that up a little bit, number 3.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, let us turn to 428 page 3, this is your statement of 1995. Page 3 of the bottom paragraph. The bottom paragraph, if we can blow that up a little bit. We start at the middle of that -- do you see that, Major, the Croats entered the town ..."

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The "The Croats entered the town around -- on the 5th of August at 1200 from the south and they obviously knew people had left the town. I can say that because they entered the town in a convoy, 7 tanks, 2 APCs which one does not do if one expects combat." Now, this was at noontime. The Croats were already in the town by 11.15, according to this ECMM report, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That's what that report said. I only saw them enter at 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when you made this statement about them entering the town at 12.00, did you know that they had entered the town earlier at 11.15?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I have several brief areas left, Judge. I have a little bit, I don't know if you wanted the break at 10.15 or if you wanted me to continue on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's ask Mr. Dijkstra as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell us if that's any different. Let's then return to the original scheduling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I shift to get another subject, Major, and I'd like to just talk to you about the testimony that you gave about ransacking that is also in paragraph 31 of P429. Now, based on your experience, sir, in the area, do you know whether or not the RSK soldiers in Knin were living in their homes and keeping weapons in their homes? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I know they were living there. I'm -- I don't know if they were keeping weapons in their house. I haven't seen any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If we can just go into closed session for a moment, Judge. Private session, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I can re-ask that question in open session, Judge, there was no need for that question to be in private is session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please then repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Bear with me, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I asked you that with regard to paragraph 30 and we were talking about you having 11 vehicles that were insufficient to do the job for UNMOs and you said that you got more vehicles; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And how many did you get?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I can look it up for you if it's really important but it should be somewhere between 10 and 15 at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: So 10 or 15 more or just 10 and 15?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, between 10 to 15 more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me turn your attention to paragraph 29 of your statement. In this, that you note that the second sentence, "I heard later from friends that there had been something on the radio telling them to leave." Now -- do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now was this a broadcast coming from the RSK forces on the radio telling people that they should leave the area?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I cannot say if it was the RSK or the Serbian government making the broadcast. The only thing I heard is that there was a broadcast on the radio to evacuate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And without giving us any names, who did you hear this from?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: People I met during the time it was still Krajina and made contact with later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: And they told you this thereafter?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No. How you mean the day after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I mean did they tell you this at the time or?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: They told me this after 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now, one last item, sir. You mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, may I seek one point of clarification. You told us that you do not know whether it was an ARSK broadcast or a Serbian government broadcast. You are, however, able apparently to tell us that it was a is Serbian broadcast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my friends told me that it was a Serbian broadcast, at least it was on those channels, as far as I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your friends told you it was Serbian but you do not have further details about what kind of Serbian broadcast it was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Even if I would have heard it, I wouldn't have understood it anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: We're going to change subjects yet again, Major, and I'd just like to talk to you about this incident of the anti-aircraft gun that you observed on the road between Knin and Drnis. Without going through it, and I look through the UNMO is situation reports for the 10th of August and a report of individuals shooting anti-aircraft guns is not in any of the situation reports neither the updates or the sitreps. Just for the record, Your Honour, I'm talking about P113, P114, and P115. Major, did -- when you observed this, did you report it to -- or do you know if it was reported to any Croatian authorities that the -- these individuals dressed in uniforms committed this act?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I can just have one moment, Major.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Major, thank you very much. Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kehoe. We'll first take a break. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late start but the breaks are just too short for our meetings. That's our problem. Mr. Mikulicic -- Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: I apologise, if we can just -- I talked to Mr. Kehoe at the break regarding 65 ter 5199 and my understanding is that there is no objection so if we could have that admitted at this stage, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That's correct. Mr. Hedaraly and I spoke, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has not been assigned a number yet. Mr. Registrar -- Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. 65 ter number 05199 will become Exhibit P434.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P434 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed. Mr. Mikulicic -- Mr. Dijkstra, Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac, and he'll now start his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Dijkstra. I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Markac, and I will have a few questions for you. I hope they won't be too much. Mr. Dijkstra, you said in your statement that before your arrival in the area of the former Yugoslavia, you attended a two to three-week intensive course for your role as UN observer. Could you please briefly describe the substance and the content of that course, that training that you underwent?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I can. Apart from redoing basic military things like nuclear or biological warfare stuff, we also got lessons in recognition in all weaponry that should have -- could be in that area. We got lessons in - how do you say - the rules or laws for combat, humanitarian rules or laws, you got quite a lot of lessons into the cultural, historical background of the former Yugoslavia, the conflict, the parties involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After your arrival on the territory of the former republic of Serbian Krajina, did you assess that the training that you underwent was sufficient for the situation that you found yourself in?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I don't understand the question completely. What do you specifically want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In some situations while you were in Benkovac when you arrived, did you run into situations that were not covered by the training that you had gone through? That was actually the gist of my question.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: There was one situation where the training will never ever could prepared me for and that was that it was very common that if you were in a meeting, you must drink alcohol and I'm a non-drinker. So that was probably the only situation where I felt pretty uncomfortable but for the rest of the training it was sufficient enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dijkstra, was there talk during the course what your attitude toward the local population should be?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Not as much in the Dutch training, but we got some additional training when we arrived in Zagreb, and the rule was that you should treat and fair -- respect their background, their personality, and -- but not to - how to say - socialise too closely, if I may put it like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Following Operation Storm, the mission of the UN observers changed. We heard this from several witnesses in this courtroom. Could you tell us, please, whether you were issued some specific instructions relating to the change to your original mandate or mission?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I can answer yes and no. To my specific task, I did not get that much change because I was the logistics officer. My task was specifically to provide the logistics for the other UNMOs to do their tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dijkstra, in your 2007/2008 statement, paragraph 6, you describe some units of the army of the Republic of Serbian Krajina among others, you mentioned that there was a training camp in Donji Bruska village that was headed by Captain Dragan and according to your information, this was the Red Berets camp. This was some sort of special unit of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. Could you tell us more about this unit and Captain Dragan who headed this camp as said in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I can't. I visited that camp only once and at that time, Captain Dragan was there only once so I have not spoken to him. The information here in this statement is what I have been informed by my colleagues who were longer in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you aware what the purpose of that unit was within the structure of the army of the republic of Serbian Krajina?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: During your stay in Benkovac, you had occasion to see police stations and police officers; am I correct? I mean the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I know which police you mean. If it helps, I can phrase my answer like this: I never interacted as an UNMO with the civilian police not because they stopped me on the roadside but also not because I had to do business with them. So if I saw them, it was just because I passed them or because I passed the police station. The only police officer we ever interacted with was the man that was watched over our vehicles when we parked them in the parking lot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you moved from Benkovac to Knin, which was toward the end of July or more specifically on the 26th of July, 1995, according to your statements you were in charge of logistics and you did not patrol the area anymore. You did mention, however, that as needed, you visited at least twice or three times a week certain localities such as Donji Lapac, Gospic, Korenica, Gracac and so on and so forth. My question is this, on these occasions when you travelled on the road from Gracac to Gospic, did you notice a large group of the 9th Gracac Brigade in the village of Gracac and their command post, did you know this and did you observe it?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: To be just clear for me are we talking Croatian troops or RSK troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are talking about the RSK troops, military units.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Okay. As a logistics officer, my travels started after Oluja. I was only there for about, what was it, ten days, so most of my time I spent with picking up the business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have I understood your answer correctly. When you arrived in Knin on the 26th of July up until the beginning of Operation Storm, at the beginning of August, you did not travel this route?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Not that I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I would like to refer you back to your 2007/2008 statement, paragraphs 37, 38 where you mention that late in August and early in September, Croatian civilians began arriving and that they looted houses and that these were in fact people who were returning to their own homes. Do you have any more specific information or more detailed information about this phenomenon?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: What do you specifically want to know?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you learn about this?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: As I told your colleague, by that time I had figured out and have been told how the Croatian licence plating system worked, so I could tell if cars were coming from Zadar, Sibenik, Split or other towns. So in the beginning, you would mostly see Zadar, Sibenik, Split licence plates but as time grew, the plates were coming from further and further, one time I even saw plates from Kula, Dubrovnik, Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 38, you mentioned that there was a lot of destruction to houses close to the border region between Croatia and Bosnia. Do you know -- are you aware, Mr. Dijkstra, and we had occasion to hear such information from various witnesses in this courtroom, that across the border from Bosnia, soldiers of the BH army and civilians in vehicles bearing registration plates of Bosnia and Herzegovina crossed the border, came into Croatia, and looted homes and took away cattle. Do you know of this?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let you now move to another topic. My learned colleague Mr. Kehoe asked you about shelling, and this is really what I wanted to ask you about as well for the most part; however, you said that you were not trained to answer those questions. As a person who was not trained in explosives and shelling, are you able to distinguish, based on the sound that you heard, whether there was a firing of a shell, an explosion of a shell, and between the echo of a shell or an impact of a shell? Were you able to distinguish those different sounds?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I cannot be 100 per cent positive to say that I would distinguish it every single time. I probably could distinguish the firing and the shelling if I was close enough to both, but an echo would be difficult, I guess. It depends on what kind of echo it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that if you were not too close to the explosion, that you could not tell between an explosion and a detonation of a grenade -- the firing and a detonation of a grenade -- shell?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: I think I would be able to make the difference between the firing and the detonation, but the firing -- of the firing and -- the detonation of the echo would probably be more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dijkstra, you said at the beginning that in relation to the mission, that the training that you underwent provided information and instructions on how to treat the local population. You also were billeted with a private -- or you had your quarters at a private home, a member of the local population; correct?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We can see from your diary, which was attached to the statement, Exhibit P432, that you had a lot of contacts with the local civilians. You had dinners with them, conversations, and so on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Depends on what you call a lot. For me a lot would be every day and it wasn't every day and especially not with locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well tell us then, how often was this, then?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: First of all, can you clarify what you call "locals" for me locals would be the civilian population; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: Locals will not be civilians working for the UN. True?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that some UN workers, I mean the interpreters and other staff were recruited from the local civilian population, that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SWITBERTUS JOHANNES DIJKSTRA
utterances.text: If we are including those in your -- the people you call "locals" then it's true I had a lot because you saw your interpreters daily and -- in a time and situation provided, you can have dinners with them or you can have a coffee with them. No -- UN personnel, I would not say I had a lot, probably occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
